neighbors.heading: a rebuke you can love
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said the person who corrects you is pointing at buried treasure. The Hebrew Bible says it too. Proverbs: "Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee; reprove a wise man, and he will love thee." And the Torah makes honest correction an act of love: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour."
neighbors.difference: In the Torah, rebuke is a commandment from God, and Jewish teachers add that it must never shame the person. In the Dhammapada, welcoming correction is part of training your own mind, with no commandment behind it.
neighbors.shared: a friend who tells you the truth kindly is a gift.

neighbors.heading: glad to be shown
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said to follow the one who corrects you like someone showing you treasure. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself in the same spirit: "If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured."
neighbors.difference: Marcus was a Stoic: he welcomed correction so his reason would follow the truth, and he wrote only to himself. The Dhammapada ties correction to a teacher you choose to follow, on a path out of suffering.
neighbors.shared: being corrected well is a kind of gift, not a defeat.

neighbors.heading: an atom's weight
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said a water-pot fills drop by drop, with harm or with good. The Qur'an counts just as small: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing is too little to count, not one kind word, not one careless one.
neighbors.difference: For the Dhammapada, deeds ripen on their own, like fruit, with no judge. In Islam, Allah sees every deed and weighs it on the Day of Judgment; the counting is His, and so is the mercy.
neighbors.shared: small kindnesses add up; none of them is wasted.

neighbors.heading: a little goes a long way
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said good gathers little by little, like water in a pot. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna something close about the path he's teaching: here no effort is lost, and nothing goes backward. Even a little of this dharma, he says, protects you from great fear.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God, and the little effort is the yoga of acting without craving the fruit. The Dhammapada names no god; the good deed itself ripens, like fruit, in its own time.
neighbors.shared: start small; small is how anything good begins.

neighbors.heading: not one harsh word
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada asked for speech as quiet as a cracked gong: no harsh words, no echo. Baba Farid, whose verses Sikhs keep in the Guru Granth Sahib, says it plainly: don't speak even one harsh word, because the true Master lives in everyone. Don't break anyone's heart; each one is a priceless jewel.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, gentle speech honors the one Creator who dwells in every heart. The Dhammapada gives a different reason: harsh words come back, and the quiet of not answering is already peace.
neighbors.shared: the words you don't say can keep the peace.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a soft answer
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said harsh words come back, and quiet ends the quarrel. The letter of James gives Christians the same order: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." And Proverbs, in the Christian Bible too: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger."
neighbors.difference: James ties gentle speech to God: human anger, he says, doesn't work the righteousness of God. The Dhammapada ties the cracked gong's quiet to nirvana, a peace reached by the one who stops answering back.
neighbors.shared: a gentle answer can end a fight before it starts.

neighbors.heading: don't become them
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said to live happily among those who hate us, without hating back. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote a one-line version in his private notebook: "The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer." He wrote it to himself, as a reminder for hard days.
neighbors.difference: Marcus refuses hatred to keep his reason and character his own. The Dhammapada adds a picture of joy: owning nothing, free of hatred, feeding on happiness like the bright gods.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to become what hurt you.

neighbors.heading: do good to them
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said, let us live happily, not hating those who hate us. Catholics hear a hard, beautiful teaching from Jesus in the Gospel: "Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you. Bless them that curse you, and pray for them that calumniate you." Not only no hatred: kindness, and a prayer.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, loving an enemy follows Jesus, who prayed from the cross for those who crucified him, and it is done with God's grace. The Dhammapada asks for a heart free of hatred, reached by training the mind.
neighbors.shared: hate doesn't have to be answered with hate.

neighbors.heading: santosha
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada called contentment the best riches. Its Pali word, santutthi, has a near twin in Sanskrit: santosha. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras list santosha among the observances, the niyamas, and promise that from contentment comes happiness nothing can surpass. Not having more. Feeling enough.
neighbors.difference: In the Yoga Sutras, santosha sits beside devotion to Ishvara, the Lord, on a path to the seer resting in itself. The Dhammapada sets contentment beside health and trust, on the road to nirvana.
neighbors.shared: enough is a kind of wealth no one can take.

neighbors.heading: who is rich?
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada called contentment the best riches. A rabbi in the Mishnah, Ben Zoma, asks: who is rich? And answers: the one who is happy with his portion. He backs it with a psalm: "When thou eatest the labour of thy hands, happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee."
neighbors.difference: Ben Zoma grounds his answer in a psalm about one who fears the Lord, so the portion is received as a blessing. The Dhammapada's contentment needs no giver; it's a mind that stops feeling poor when there's enough.
neighbors.shared: rich is a feeling of enough, not a number.

neighbors.heading: the speck and the beam
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said we winnow other people's faults like chaff and hide our own. Jesus used a picture just as sharp: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" First take out the beam, he says; then you'll see clearly enough to help.
neighbors.difference: Jesus speaks within a call to leave judgment to God, who will measure you as you measure others. The Dhammapada says fault-finding feeds your own passions; the harm is in what it does to your mind.
neighbors.shared: the faults easiest to see are rarely our own.

neighbors.heading: cover, don't hunt
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said the fault-finder scatters a neighbor's faults like chaff. The Qur'an asks believers to stop the hunt: "Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime. And spy not, neither backbite one another." And the Prophet taught that whoever covers a fellow Muslim's fault, Allah will cover theirs on the Day of Resurrection.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, covering another's fault is answered by Allah's own covering. The Dhammapada names no judge: looking for others' faults simply makes your own passions grow.
neighbors.shared: hold others' faults gently; you have some of your own.

neighbors.heading: the other cheek
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada pictured an elephant in battle, bearing arrows without striking back. Catholics hear Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount: "if one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other." And Saint Peter remembers Jesus himself: "Who, when he was reviled, did not revile: when he suffered, he threatened not."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, bearing insult is a way of following Jesus on the road to the cross, with God's help. The Dhammapada's elephant bears arrows because a tamed mind no longer needs to strike back.
neighbors.shared: you can take a hard word without throwing one back.

neighbors.heading: don't strike back
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said to bear harsh words the way a war elephant bears arrows. Baba Farid, whose verses Sikhs keep in the Guru Granth Sahib, puts it plainly: if someone hits you with their fists, don't turn and hit them back. Kiss their feet, he says, and go home.
neighbors.difference: Farid speaks as a lover of God, humble because the Lord lives in everyone. Sikhs also honor the saint-soldier, who defends others when wrong can't be stopped another way. The Dhammapada's elephant bears arrows through a mind it has trained.
neighbors.shared: strength sometimes looks like not hitting back.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: never full
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada pictured craving as a creeper, and a monkey grabbing fruit after fruit. Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible, watched the same restless hunger: "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing." And: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver." More never quite finishes the job.
neighbors.difference: Ecclesiastes ends by turning to God: fear God, and keep his commandments. The Dhammapada's answer is to see craving clearly and pull it up by the root, through a path of practice.
neighbors.shared: more rarely feels like enough; noticing that is a start.

neighbors.heading: the treadmill
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said craving leaps like a monkey, from fruit to fruit. Psychologists have a name for that leap: the hedonic treadmill. Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell argued that people get used to good things, so the thrill fades and we reach for the next one, running hard and staying in place.
neighbors.difference: The psychology describes the treadmill; it doesn't promise a way off. The Dhammapada says craving is the root of suffering, and that it can be pulled up through a whole path of practice.
neighbors.shared: wanting the next thing is human; noticing it is freeing.
neighbors.sources: Brickman & Campbell, "Hedonic relativism and planning the good society" (1971) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the noblest of you
neighbors.text: Today the Dhammapada said no one is noble by birth, only by deeds. The Qur'an speaks to all people at once: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct."
neighbors.difference: In Islam, nobility is measured in the sight of Allah, by conduct that keeps Him in mind. The Dhammapada measures it by a mind that has put evil away and cut the stream of craving.
neighbors.shared: who you are is in how you live, not where you're from.

neighbors.heading: who is a brahmin?
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said one becomes a brahmin by deeds, not birth. The Mahabharata has a moment like it. A great serpent asks Yudhishthira: who is a brahmin? He answers: one in whom truth, giving, forgiveness, good conduct, gentleness, austerity and mercy are seen. And if those are found in someone born a shudra, he says, that person is no shudra.
neighbors.difference: Hindu traditions hold more than one view: many texts and communities tie varna to birth, while passages like this put conduct first. The Buddha's verses keep the honored word and open it to anyone, by deeds alone.
neighbors.shared: goodness is earned in how you live, day after day.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Yudhishthira and the serpent Nahusha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good of all
neighbors.text: Today we met mudita, the gladness that someone else is doing well. Sikhs close the Ardas, their shared prayer, with a wish for the whole world: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, may spirits rise; by your will, may everyone prosper. Not just my people. Sarbat: all.
neighbors.difference: The Ardas asks God, by his will, for the good of all. Mudita isn't a prayer to anyone; it's gladness practiced in the heart, widening from a dear friend to a stranger to someone difficult.
neighbors.shared: wishing everyone well leaves less room for envy.
neighbors.sources: Ardas, the Sikh prayer, closing line (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rejoice with them
neighbors.text: Today we met mudita, gladness at someone else's good news. Paul gives Christians the same instruction in one line: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." And in his hymn to love, he names mudita's old enemy: "charity envieth not."
neighbors.difference: For Paul, shared joy comes from belonging to one body in Christ, members one of another. Mudita is trained on its own, widening step by step from a friend to someone difficult.
neighbors.shared: someone else's good day can be yours too.

neighbors.heading: not the thing, the opinion
neighbors.text: Today we met upekkha, equanimity: balance that doesn't abandon anyone. The Stoics trained a kind of balance too. The teacher Epictetus put it in one sentence: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Change the opinion, and the storm quiets.
neighbors.difference: Stoic calm rests on what is in your control: your own judgments. Upekkha rests on seeing that beings own their actions, and it keeps kindness and compassion close, so balance never turns into not caring.
neighbors.shared: steady doesn't mean cold; you can care and stay calm.

neighbors.heading: sun on everyone
neighbors.text: Today we met upekkha, a balance that sees every being as equal, like someone on a hill seeing the whole valley. Jesus points Catholics to the sky for the same picture: God "maketh his sun to rise upon the good and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust." Love, he says, doesn't pick favorites.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, this even love is God's own, and people share in it as his children, by grace. Upekkha isn't modeled on God; it grows from seeing that every being owns its own actions.
neighbors.shared: sunlight doesn't check who deserves it.

neighbors.heading: walking, sleeping, breathing
neighbors.text: Today the sutta said: walking, know you're walking; sitting, know you're sitting. The Bhagavad Gita has its own list of ordinary moments. The one who knows the truth, Krishna says, thinks "I do nothing at all," while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping and breathing, letting the senses move among their objects.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the knower rests as the self that doesn't act, steady while the body moves. The sutta asks only that you know each posture as it is, without clinging to a self behind it.
neighbors.shared: the plainest moments of a day can be a practice.

neighbors.heading: sitting, walking, lying down
neighbors.text: Today the sutta named the four postures: walking, standing, sitting, lying down. Jews say the Shema evening and morning, and its words cover the same ground: "and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."
neighbors.difference: In the Shema, what you carry through every posture is God's words, and love for him with all your heart. The sutta asks only that you know the body as it is, walking or sitting, without clinging.
neighbors.shared: any posture, any hour, can hold a moment of remembering.

neighbors.heading: dust and days
neighbors.text: Today the sutta said, gently: this body too will end. Many Christians keep a day for that truth. On Ash Wednesday, foreheads are marked with ashes, echoing Genesis: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." And a psalm turns it into a prayer: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, remembering death sits beside hope in the resurrection of Jesus and life with God. The sutta makes no such promise; it uses the body's change to loosen clinging and wake up now.
neighbors.shared: remembering life is short can make today matter more.

neighbors.heading: every soul will taste it
neighbors.text: Today the sutta said, gently: this body too is of that nature. The Qur'an says it plainly: "Every soul will taste of death." And the Prophet Muhammad told his companions to remember often the one that cuts every pleasure short: death. Not to darken the day, but to keep the heart awake in it.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, death is a return to Allah, opening onto the Day of Resurrection, when every deed is weighed. The sutta points to no judge; seeing the body change loosens the mind's grip.
neighbors.shared: life is short, so today deserves your whole heart.

neighbors.heading: naming the roots
neighbors.text: Today the sutta named five hindrances that cloud the mind, from desire to doubt. Catholics keep a list too: the capital sins, pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth. The Catechism calls them capital because they give rise to other sins. Naming them, in an examination of conscience, helps you see them coming.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics these are sins, turnings away from God, healed by grace and confession. The hindrances aren't offenses against anyone; they're patterns to notice arising and passing, then let go.
neighbors.shared: what you can name, you can begin to let go.

neighbors.heading: five thieves
neighbors.text: Today the sutta named five hindrances that cover a clear mind. Sikhs know a list of five too: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Gurbani calls them five thieves living inside the body, robbing what's precious within. Knowing who they are is the start of guarding the house.
neighbors.difference: In Sikh teaching, the five thieves are overcome by remembering the Name and by the Guru's grace. The sutta's hindrances fade through noticing: know when one comes, how it goes, and how it stays gone.
neighbors.shared: the hardest thieves to catch are the ones inside.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: only for myself?
neighbors.text: Today the Heart Sutra said nothing stands alone; a cup is made of clay, fire and hands. Jewish teaching sees people woven together too. Hillel asked: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? But if I am only for myself, what am I? And the Talmud says all Israel are responsible for one another.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, God is the one Creator, and people are bound to each other by covenant and care. The Heart Sutra speaks of everything, not only people: nothing has a being of its own, apart from everything else.
neighbors.shared: no one makes it alone; we hold each other up.

neighbors.heading: the bond is holy
neighbors.text: Today the Heart Sutra said form is emptiness: nothing stands on its own. Marcus Aurelius saw a web too: "All things are implicated with one another, and the bond is holy; and there is hardly anything unconnected with any other thing." Look at your breakfast and count the hands.
neighbors.difference: For the Stoics, everything is joined because one reason, the logos, orders the whole cosmos. The Heart Sutra names no ordering reason; things depend on each other, and none has a self of its own.
neighbors.shared: everything you touch carries the work of countless others.

neighbors.heading: no fear, no grief
neighbors.text: Today the Heart Sutra said a mind with no walls has no fear. The Qur'an speaks of people free of fear too: "Lo! verily the friends of Allah are (those) on whom fear (cometh) not, nor do they grieve." The next verse says who they are: those who believe and keep their duty.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, freedom from fear comes from nearness to Allah, trusting the One who holds everything. In the Heart Sutra, it comes from wisdom, seeing that the walls fear guards were never solid.
neighbors.shared: fear can loosen its grip, even if it never fully leaves.

neighbors.heading: fear comes from a second
neighbors.text: Today the Heart Sutra said: no walls around the mind, no fear. An Upanishad tells of the first being, alone and afraid, who then thinks: there is nothing but me, so what is there to fear? Fear, it says, comes from a second, from something set apart. Another Upanishad adds: one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishads find freedom from fear in Brahman, the one reality, which many Hindu teachers call your deepest self. The Heart Sutra finds it in emptiness: nothing standing apart, and no single ground beneath.
neighbors.shared: fear shrinks when the world stops feeling like the other side of a wall.

items.lessonTitle: Every day is a good day

neighbors.heading: sweet is your will
neighbors.text: Today Yunmen said: every day is a good day. Not every pleasant day; this one, as it comes. Sikhs sing a line from Guru Arjan in the same spirit: tera keea meetha laage, whatever you do seems sweet to me. Living in the hukam, God's order, means meeting the day you're given.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the day is sweet because it comes from God's will, accepted with love. Yunmen's good day has no giver; it's simply this day, met fully, nothing added.
neighbors.shared: this day, just as it is, is the one to live.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: this is the day
neighbors.text: Today Yunmen said: every day is a good day. Christians sing a psalm with the same face turned toward today: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." And Jesus says not to borrow tomorrow's trouble: "Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the day is good because God made it and gives it. Yunmen's good day isn't a gift from anyone; it's just this day, lived without wishing it were another.
neighbors.shared: today is enough; you don't have to live tomorrow yet.

neighbors.heading: to the woods
neighbors.text: Today we met the Thai forest monks, walking into the jungle to live simply and sit. An American writer went to the woods for his own reasons. Henry David Thoreau wrote: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach."
neighbors.difference: Thoreau's cabin was a personal experiment in simple living, written up as a book. The forest monks keep an old monastic code under a teacher, and practice for freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the quiet woods show you what you really need.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (1854)

neighbors.heading: into the desert
neighbors.text: Today we met forest monks who keep the old rules in the wild. Catholics remember the desert fathers. Saint Athanasius tells of Antony, who heard the Gospel say "go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor," and did it, and in time went into the Egyptian desert to pray. Others followed him there.
neighbors.difference: Antony went to the desert to seek God in prayer and resist temptation by Christ's grace. The forest monks go to train the mind and see clearly, following the Buddha's path.
neighbors.shared: some people go into the quiet so they can bring something back.

neighbors.heading: the guest as god
neighbors.text: Today we saw an old exchange: villagers give monks food and robes, and monks give teaching. Hindu homes know a giving like it. The Taittiriya Upanishad sends a student home with this advice: let your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest be to you as gods. Give with faith, give with modesty, give with care.
neighbors.difference: In this Hindu teaching, a guest at the door is honored as if God had come. In Theravada, giving, dana, earns merit and keeps a renunciant life possible, and the monks give the teaching back.
neighbors.shared: giving and receiving can hold a whole town together.

neighbors.heading: zebulun and issachar
neighbors.text: Today we saw monks and villagers holding each other up. Jewish tradition tells of two tribes doing the same. Zebulun went to sea and traded; Issachar sat and studied Torah. Rashi says Zebulun brought food to Issachar's table, and that's why Moses blessed Zebulun first. One works, one learns, and tradition says they share the reward.
neighbors.difference: In the Jewish story, both partners keep homes and families, and the learning is Torah, God's teaching. Theravada monks leave home, and the village supports a life given wholly to the Buddha's path.
neighbors.shared: the one who works and the one who learns need each other.

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today we met om mani padme hum, a mantra said over and over until it lives in the breath. Many Eastern Orthodox Christians keep a short prayer the same way: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, repeated through the day. It answers Paul's line: "Pray without ceasing."
neighbors.difference: The Jesus Prayer calls on Jesus, worshipped by Christians as God's Son. The mantra calls on Avalokiteshvara, a bodhisattva of compassion, and Tibetan teachers explain it as growing compassion and wisdom in the one who says it.
neighbors.shared: a few words, repeated with love, can steady a whole day.
neighbors.sources: 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (KJV) · the Jesus Prayer, Eastern Orthodox tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today we met om mani padme hum, said again and again, on beads, under the breath. Muslims know that rhythm as dhikr, remembrance: short phrases like subhan Allah and alhamdulillah, counted on beads or fingers. The Qur'an says why: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Dhikr remembers Allah, the One God, through His names and praise. The six syllables call on Avalokiteshvara, a bodhisattva, and Tibetan teachers explain them as growing compassion and wisdom in the one who says them.
neighbors.shared: a word said with love, again and again, can quiet the heart.

neighbors.heading: by their fruits
neighbors.text: Today Tibetan teaching said: check a teacher carefully, even for years, before you trust them. Jesus gives Catholics a test for the same job: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. By their fruits you shall know them." Look at the life, not only the words.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, a teacher is tested by their fruits and by the faith the Church has handed down. In Tibetan Buddhism, a student tests a lama personally, then may receive practices from that one teacher.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher's life matches their words; it's okay to check.

neighbors.heading: earn, and give
neighbors.text: Today Tibetan teaching said: examine a teacher before you trust them. Guru Nanak gives a sharp test. Someone who calls himself a guru or a pir and goes around begging, he says, don't touch his feet. The one who eats what he earns by his own work, and gives some away, knows the way.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs bow to no living person as Guru now; the Guru Granth Sahib itself is the Guru. In Tibetan Buddhism, a living lama, carefully chosen, is central to the practice.
neighbors.shared: a true teacher is known by how they live, not their title.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two are better than one
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said a good friend is the whole of the holy life. Jewish teaching prizes friends too. Ecclesiastes: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow." And the Mishnah says: make yourself a teacher, and acquire a friend.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish tradition, friends often learn Torah in pairs, chavruta, helping each other keep God's commandments. The Buddha's admirable friend helps you walk the eightfold path, and he names himself as that friend.
neighbors.shared: the right friend lifts you up when you fall.

neighbors.heading: no one would choose it
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said good friendship is the whole of the holy life. Aristotle, the Greek philosopher, opens his books on friendship by saying no one would choose to live without friends, even with every other good thing. The best kind, he says, is between good people who wish each other well for the friend's own sake.
neighbors.difference: For Aristotle, friendship between good people is part of a flourishing human life. The Buddha's admirable friend points further, toward freedom from suffering, from birth, aging and death.
neighbors.shared: a friend who makes you better is one of life's great gifts.

neighbors.heading: no compulsion
neighbors.text: Today the teaching called itself ehipassiko: come and see, not come and believe. The Qur'an makes room for that freedom too: "There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error." Faith, in this verse, can't be forced on anyone.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an invites people to believe in Allah, trusting the right way to be clear to those who look. Ehipassiko asks for no belief first; it invites you to try the practice and see for yourself.
neighbors.shared: what's true can be offered; it never has to be forced.

neighbors.heading: then do as you choose
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha's teaching said: come and see; the seeing is yours. The Bhagavad Gita ends its teaching with an open door too. Krishna tells Arjuna: I have given you this wisdom, more secret than any secret. Reflect on it fully, then do as you choose.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God and then invites Arjuna to take refuge in him. The Buddha's "come and see" points to a practice anyone can test, with the Buddha as a guide who shows the way.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher gives you the map and lets you choose.

items.lessonTitle: Year one close: the big lookout

neighbors.heading: no end to it
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha held up a handful of leaves: the forest is always bigger. Guru Nanak's Japji says it too: worlds below worlds, skies above skies, and seekers grow tired searching for the edge. There's no end to the praises, he sings, and no end to those who speak them. The more you learn, the bigger it gets.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the endlessness belongs to Waheguru, God, whose greatness no one can measure. The Buddha's forest is all he came to know; his handful is what helps end suffering.
neighbors.shared: there's always more ahead, and what you have is enough to walk.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauris 22 and 24, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: more than the world could hold
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha said his teaching is a handful of leaves from a whole forest. John's Gospel ends the same way: "there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books." What is written, John says, was chosen so you might believe and have life.
neighbors.difference: John's handful is written so readers might believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The Buddha's handful is the four truths, given so people can end suffering by walking the path themselves.
neighbors.shared: you don't need every leaf to start walking.
